snapshots.label: 313 to 399
snapshots.title: Imperial support and growing church authority
snapshots.summary: Roman emperors supported Christianity while bishops gained influence; imperial law both protected and restricted Jewish life.
snapshots.jewish: Jewish legal protection coexisted with restrictions; bishops and emperors did not always agree about enforcement.

snapshots.label: 400 to 499
snapshots.title: Imperial law and episcopal authority
snapshots.summary: Roman emperors issued laws on Jews, while Rome's bishops claimed a distinct religious authority.
snapshots.jewish: Laws recognized Jewish religious life while restricting offices and other activities; local enforcement varied.

snapshots.label: 500 to 599
snapshots.title: Gregory I and legal Jewish worship
snapshots.summary: Frankish kings and Roman bishops held different powers; Gregory I defended legal Jewish worship while seeking conversions.
snapshots.jewish: Gregory opposed coercive baptism and interference with lawful worship, without recognizing religious equality.

snapshots.label: 600 to 699
snapshots.title: Visigothic kings and Toledo councils
snapshots.summary: Catholic Visigothic kings and Toledo councils imposed conversion rules and restrictions on Jewish religious life.
snapshots.jewish: The Fourth Council opposed forced baptism but required Jews already baptized to remain Christian.

snapshots.label: 700 to 799
snapshots.title: Frankish alliance and papal territories
snapshots.summary: Frankish kings and Roman popes formed an alliance; territorial grants expanded papal government in central Italy.
snapshots.jewish: A distinct immediate change for Jewish residents caused by these territorial grants is not established.

snapshots.label: 800 to 899
snapshots.title: Carolingian protection and episcopal opposition
snapshots.summary: Louis the Pious protected Jewish merchants, while Archbishop Agobard of Lyon challenged their privileges.
snapshots.jewish: Some Jews received royal privileges that a local archbishop opposed; royal and ecclesiastical positions differed.

snapshots.label: 900 to 999
snapshots.title: Local rulers and papal conversion policy
snapshots.summary: German kings, local bishops, and Roman nobles shaped authority; Leo VII addressed conversion and expulsion.
snapshots.jewish: Leo VII rejected forced baptism but authorized expulsion for refusing conversion; no completed expulsion is established.

snapshots.label: 1000 to 1099
snapshots.title: Settlement privileges and crusading violence
snapshots.summary: German emperors and bishops granted Jewish privileges, while crusading bands attacked communities along the Rhine.
snapshots.jewish: Some bishops offered protection, but Jewish communities also suffered killings and forced baptism during the First Crusade.

snapshots.label: 1100 to 1199
snapshots.title: Papal protection and royal jurisdiction
snapshots.summary: Popes issued protection letters, while kings governed Jewish residence and crusading remained a source of danger.
snapshots.jewish: Papal protection opposed forced baptism and attacks, but did not grant equal status or guarantee local safety.

snapshots.label: 1200 to 1299
snapshots.title: Council restrictions and royal expulsion
snapshots.summary: Innocent III's council imposed distinctions; kings such as Edward I controlled residence and ordered expulsions.
snapshots.jewish: Dress rules and royal restrictions varied by jurisdiction; Edward I expelled Jews from England in 1290.

snapshots.label: 1300 to 1399
snapshots.title: Papal protection during plague and violence
snapshots.summary: Avignon popes and European kings held separate powers; Clement VI opposed false plague accusations against Jews.
snapshots.jewish: Protection letters did not prevent attacks everywhere; Iberian communities later suffered violence and forced conversion.

snapshots.label: 1400 to 1499
snapshots.title: Iberian monarchy and Jewish expulsion
snapshots.summary: Iberian monarchs and inquisitions increased pressure; Ferdinand and Isabella ordered Jewish expulsion in 1492.
snapshots.jewish: Jews had to leave the monarchs' realms or convert; baptized people suspected of Jewish practice faced inquisitorial scrutiny.

snapshots.label: 1500 to 1599
snapshots.title: Papal segregation and Tuscan privileges
snapshots.summary: Popes ruled central Italian territories; Paul IV imposed segregation, while Medici rulers offered privileges at Livorno.
snapshots.jewish: Jewish conditions differed between papal jurisdictions and Tuscan ports; no single Italian policy applied everywhere.

snapshots.label: 1600 to 1699
snapshots.title: Italian ghettos and colonial inquisitions
snapshots.summary: Popes governed Rome, Venice regulated its ghetto, and the Spanish crown's Mexican Inquisition prosecuted conversos.
snapshots.jewish: Italian confinement continued, while inquisitorial prosecutions disrupted converso families in colonial Mexico.

snapshots.label: 1700 to 1799
snapshots.title: Baptism policy and Habsburg reforms
snapshots.summary: Benedict XIV maintained baptism rules in Rome; Joseph II eased some restrictions in Habsburg lands.
snapshots.jewish: Jewish families faced baptism-related custody risks, while selected Habsburg reforms widened education and occupations.

snapshots.label: 1800 to 1899
snapshots.title: Papal government and Italian unification
snapshots.summary: Papal government defended baptism policy, while Italian unification ended the pope's territorial rule over Rome.
snapshots.jewish: The Mortara case separated a Jewish child from his parents; Rome's Jews gained civil emancipation after annexation.

snapshots.label: 1900 to 1999
snapshots.title: Vatican II and a change in official teaching
snapshots.summary: Popes led a worldwide church; Vatican II changed teaching about Jews, and John Paul II visited Rome's synagogue.
snapshots.jewish: Official Catholic teaching rejected collective Jewish guilt and supported dialogue; local attitudes did not change uniformly.

snapshots.label: 2000 to 2020
snapshots.title: Dialogue and the question of mission
snapshots.summary: Popes supported Jewish-Catholic dialogue; a Vatican commission rejected an organized Catholic mission directed at Jews.
snapshots.jewish: Dialogue expanded while theological disagreements remained; the 2015 reflection did not end every form of Christian witness.
